analysis.one_liner: Replaces the child tax deduction with an $800 refundable credit, boosts the earned income credit, and raises taxes on high incomes.
analysis.headline: Senator Gore's bill to create an $800-per-child refundable credit and raise taxes on incomes above $150,000 was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 1991 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the income tax deduction for each child under 18 with a refundable credit of up to $800 per child, meaning even families who owe no income tax would get cash back. It would have increased the earned income credit, a wage supplement for low-income workers, and allowed families to receive those credits in quarterly advance payments during the year instead of waiting for a tax refund. To pay for it, the bill would have raised top tax rates to 35%, added an 11% surtax on incomes above roughly $150,000 to $250,000, and increased the alternative minimum tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with children, especially low- and middle-income earners. A refundable per-child credit puts cash in the hands of families whose tax bill is already zero, something a deduction cannot do. Expanding the earned income credit raises take-home pay for low-wage workers, and advance payments would spread the money across the year rather than delivering it as a lump-sum refund at tax time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income working families with children

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable credit of up to $800 for each child under 18, replacing the per-child personal exemption deduction, with annual inflation adjustments [S2][S3].
Increases the earned income credit, phasing in credit rates up to 32% of earnings for families with three or more children by 1994, up from the rates then in law [S2][S3].

Requires the Treasury to make quarterly advance payments of the earned income credit and the child credit, with special procedures to reach families with incomes of $12,000 or less, so help arrives during the year rather than as a year-end refund [S2][S3].
Repeals the limits on itemized deductions and the phaseout of personal exemptions that claw back benefits from higher earners [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-income households. The bill would raise the top individual rate from 28% to 35%, impose an 11% surtax phased in above thresholds of $150,000 to $250,000 of income depending on filing status, raise the alternative minimum tax rate from 24% to 29%, and apply the surtax to estates and trusts as well [S2][S3]. Families that currently deduct a large child exemption at high marginal rates would lose that deduction in exchange for the credit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill swaps the per-child exemption deduction for the credit. A family with one child currently shielding roughly $2,000 of income from tax through the exemption would take a net tax increase unless the credit fully offset the loss, which is why the bill is partly a revenue raiser aimed at upper incomes [S3].

The credit is limited to the greater of $400 or 20% of the family's earned income plus cash child support received, so families with very little earned income get the smallest benefit, and the design ties help to earnings rather than providing it universally [S3].

Advance payments require families to estimate next year's refund; if their income changes, they could receive payments they must later reconcile with the IRS, and a smaller-than-estimated refund would come due at tax time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: cash help for families raising children on modest wages, paid for by higher taxes on the top few percent of earners. The credit's floor of $400 and its tie to earned income mean the deepest-poverty households get the least, and the advance-payment system carries real reconciliation risk for families with unstable incomes. On balance the design directs substantially more help to low- and middle-income working families than the deduction system it replaces.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Albert Gore Jr. introduced the Working Family Tax Relief Act of 1991 on May 7, 1991 [S1][S5].
Four Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced [S3][S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and estates and trusts came out ahead: the surtax, the higher 35% rate, and the increased alternative minimum tax never took effect. Working families gained nothing because the child credit and the expanded earned income credit never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households that would have paid the surtax

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll-call record exists; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their top rate to 35%, added an 11% surtax above their income thresholds, and increased the alternative minimum tax from 24% to 29%. Because the bill died, they avoided these increases while working families lost the proposed credits.
The bill applied both the new 35% top rate and the high-income surtax to estates and trusts. Neither took effect.
